e.etymology: A spelling of Delaney, an Irish surname from O Dubhshlaine, 'descendant of Dubhshlaine', a name beginning with dubh, 'dark'. A Norman source, de l'aunaie, 'from the alder grove', is also proposed.
The Yiddish form of Rachel, Hebrew for 'ewe'. In Genesis Rachel is the beloved wife of Jacob and the mother of Joseph and Benjamin. This form is used in Orthodox Jewish communities.
e.note: The ch is the throaty kh of Yiddish and Hebrew; outsiders tend to read it as Rochelle or Rachel.

e.etymology: From the English word for a light mist, or a short form of Hazel. For boys it is a recent word name in the manner of Blaze and Chase, close in sound to Hayes.

assoc.t: haze, a light mist or smog
Purple Haze, the Jimi Hendrix song
hazing, rough initiation rites for newcomers

e.note: Haze is also the name of a well-known family of cannabis strains, and hazing means abusive initiation.

e.etymology: Spanish, Portuguese and Italian form of Gilbert, a Norman name from Germanic gisil, 'pledge', and berht, 'bright'.

assoc.t: Joao and Astrud Gilberto, bossa nova stars (surname)

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Riagain, 'descendant of Riagan', a name of uncertain meaning. Shakespeare used Regan for one of King Lear's treacherous daughters. Reagan is the more common spelling today.

assoc.t: Regan, the possessed girl in The Exorcist
Regan, a cruel daughter in Shakespeare's King Lear
sounds like President Ronald Reagan

e.etymology: A spelling of Vivian and Vivienne, from the Latin name Vivianus, from vivus, 'alive'. This form is established in Swedish, where it is also read as Vivi plus Anne.
A spelling of Aaliyah, the feminine of Arabic Ali, 'high, exalted'. It also overlaps with Hebrew Aliyah, 'ascent'. The singer Aaliyah made the name widespread in the 1990s.
A pet form of Alison, Alice, Alexandra, Alyssa and other names beginning with Al-. It is also given as a name in its own right; Allie is the more common spelling.
namesakes: Ally McBeal (title lawyer of the 1990s TV series)

assoc.t: Ally, the online bank and auto lender
ally, the ordinary word for a supporter or partner
Ally McBeal, lawyer of the 1990s TV series

e.etymology: From French destin, 'destiny, fate', used as a boys' counterpart to Destiny. Destin is also a surname and the name of a beach city on the Florida Panhandle.

assoc.t: Destin, beach resort city on the Florida Panhandle

e.etymology: From the country, Latin Italia. A long-standing theory traces the name to an Oscan word meaning 'land of young cattle'. As a girls' name it follows Asia, India and Ireland.

assoc.t: Italy, the country

e.etymology: In Afrikaans it is a short form of Adriaan, the Dutch Adrian. In the US it is mostly chosen by Indian American families, as a name that sounds like Ryan and Rayan.
A late 20th-century name, explained as a short form of Letitia, Venetia and other names ending in -tia. It is also used as a short form of Tiana and Tatiana.

assoc.t: Tia Maria, coffee liqueur

e.note: Tia is the everyday word for aunt in Spanish and Portuguese.

e.etymology: French diminutive of Nicole, the feminine of Nicolas, from Greek Nikolaos: nike, 'victory', plus laos, 'people'. Nicolette is the heroine of the medieval French romance Aucassin and Nicolette.
e.note: Close in sound to Nicorette, the nicotine gum brand.

e.etymology: A spelling of Denise used in Latin America and by Spanish-speaking families in the US. Denise is the French feminine of Denis, from Dionysius, 'devoted to Dionysus', the Greek god of wine.
From Classical Nahuatl citlalli, star, the language of the Aztecs. It reached the United States through Mexican families, who use it in Spanish.

assoc.t: ice-wielding shaman in the game Genshin Impact

e.etymology: Usually traced to Latin aurum, gold, or oriri, to rise. Oriana is the beloved of the knight in the medieval romance Amadis of Gaul, and English poets used the name for Queen Elizabeth I.
namesakes: Oriana Fallaci (Italian journalist and war correspondent)

e.etymology: A modern Hebrew name, the feminine form of Aviv, spring. The word names the season of new grain and also appears in Tel Aviv.

assoc.t: Aviva, the inventor on PBS Kids' Wild Kratts

e.etymology: From the flowering shrub, which Linnaeus named in Latin for the Jesuit botanist Georg Kamel. It joined the other flower names given to girls in the 19th century.

assoc.t: camellia, the flowering shrub; Alabama's state flower

e.etymology: An English phonetic spelling of Irish Sean, which came through Old French Jehan from Latin Johannes and Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. It is the Irish John.
namesakes: Shaun Cassidy (1970s teen idol and TV producer)

assoc.t: Shaun the Sheep, Aardman's animated sheep
Shaun of the Dead, 2004 zombie comedy film

e.etymology: A modern variant of Tristan with the ending of Christian. Tristan comes from the Celtic name Drustan and was reshaped in Old French by triste, sad; he is the tragic knight of the Tristan and Isolde legend.
e.note: Often misread as Tristan or heard as Christian, so expect to spell it out.

e.etymology: A spelling of Axel that matches the English word axle. Axel is the Scandinavian form of the biblical Absalom, Hebrew for father of peace.

assoc.t: axle, the shaft a vehicle's wheels turn on
Axl Rose, Guns N' Roses singer (same sound)

e.note: Spelled exactly like the car part; Axel is the traditional spelling of the name.

e.etymology: From Arabic nuri, luminous, formed from nur, light; a traditional men's name in Arabic and Turkish. In Korean, Nuri is a separate name from a native word for the world.
The French short form of Azelie, written Zelie with an accent in France. American Catholics took it up after the 2015 canonization of Saint Zelie Martin, mother of Saint Therese of Lisieux.

assoc.t: Zelie, heroine of the novel Children of Blood and Bone

e.etymology: From a Norman baronial surname taken from the town of Vernon in Normandy, whose name comes from Gaulish verna, alder. It became a first name in the 19th century.
namesakes: Vernon Jordan (civil rights leader and presidential adviser)

e.etymology: From the Welsh word bryn, hill, found in many Welsh place names. It became a first name in Wales in the late 1800s.
e.note: In Wales Bryn is a man's name; in the United States it is given mostly to girls.

e.etymology: A Scottish surname from a medieval short form of Gregor, the Scots form of Gregory, from Greek gregorios, watchful. Actress Greer Garson, who bore her mother's maiden name, popularized it as a first name.
namesakes: Greer Garson (Oscar-winning star of Mrs. Miniver)

e.etymology: From Arabic sidra, the lote tree, recalling Sidrat al-Muntaha, the tree that marks the farthest boundary of the seventh heaven in Islamic tradition. Some also connect it with Latin sidera, stars.
e.note: Sidra is the Spanish word for cider.

e.etymology: An English form of Irish Bairre, short for Fionnbharr, from fionn, fair or white, and barr, head. It has also served as a pet form of Bartholomew.
namesakes: Barry Bonds (baseball's career home run leader)

assoc.t: Barry, HBO dark comedy about a hitman

e.etymology: A short form of Theresa and Tessa. Theresa's source is uncertain; it is usually linked to Greek therizein, to harvest, or to the Greek island of Therasia.
namesakes: Tess Durbeyfield (heroine of Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles)

e.etymology: From Irish Fionnan, a pet form of fionn, fair or white. Two 6th-century Irish saints bore it, Finnian of Clonard and Finnian of Movilla.

e.meaning: holds the heel; a form of Jacob
e.etymology: The Aramaic form of Ya'akov, Jacob, so it shares Jacob's meaning. Jewish families give it in honor of Rabbi Akiva, the great sage of the 2nd century.
namesakes: Akiva Goldsman (Oscar-winning screenwriter of A Beautiful Mind)
Akiva Schaffer (Lonely Island comedian and director)

e.etymology: A Spanish surname for families from Zamora, a medieval city in northwestern Spain. Its use as a girls' first name is recent and American.

assoc.t: Zamora, city and province in northwestern Spain
